docs.title: Point Clouds: Geometry and Spread in 2D
docs.text: My approach: I draw one fixed set of standard-normal samples and turn it into a cloud with x = μ + (s·σ)·z. Because the base draws z are reused for every scale, s = 1 reproduces item A exactly and each larger s is the same cloud simply spread wider around an unchanged mean — which is what item B asks for. All numbers below come from the script at the end of the exercise.

docs.title: A — Generate the clouds
docs.text:
I generated 400 samples (100 per class) from independent Gaussians with the given per-axis means and standard deviations:

Class Mean Std 0 \([2, 3]\) \([0.8, 2.5]\) 1 \([5, 6]\) \([1.2, 1.9]\) 2 \([8, 1]\) \([0.9, 0.9]\) 3 \([15, 4]\) \([0.5, 2.0]\)

Figure 1 — Four Gaussian clouds (\(s = 1\)). The black X markers are the class means \(\mu_0 \dots \mu_3\).

The clouds match the parameters: Class 0 is tall and narrow (large \(\sigma_y\)), Class 2 is compact and round, Class 3 is a thin vertical strip far to the right.

docs.title: B — More or less spread out
docs.text:
I regenerated the same four classes at \(s \in \{0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0\}\), scaling every standard deviation while holding the means fixed. Plotted on shared axes so the comparison is honest:

Figure 2 — The four classes at \(s = 0.5, 1, 2, 4\) on identical axes. At \(s = 0.5\) the clouds are tight islands; by \(s = 4\) they bleed across the whole plane.

docs.title: Separation ratios \(r_{ij}\) at \(s = 1\)
docs.text:
Using \(\bar{\sigma}_k = (\sigma_{k,x} + \sigma_{k,y})/2\) — so \(\bar{\sigma} = [1.65, 1.55, 0.90, 1.25]\) — the six pairwise ratios \(r_{ij} = \Vert \mu_i - \mu_j \Vert / (\bar{\sigma}_i + \bar{\sigma}_j)\) are:

Pair \((i, j)\) \(\Vert \mu_i - \mu_j \Vert\) \(r_{ij}\) (0, 1) 4.243 1.326 (1, 2) 5.831 2.380 (0, 2) 6.325 2.480 (2, 3) 7.616 3.542 (1, 3) 10.198 3.642 (0, 3) 13.038 4.496

The smallest ratio is the pair (0, 1) at \(r_{01} = 1.326\) — Classes 0 and 1 are the closest relative to their spread, exactly the overlap visible in Figure 1. Since the means are fixed, \(r_{ij}\) scales with \(1/s\), so at \(s = 2\) this smallest ratio halves to \(r_{01} = 0.663\) — no new data needed.

docs.title: Mixing rate per scale
docs.text:
The mixing rate is the fraction of points whose nearest class mean is not their own class (a purely geometric check against the four fixed means, nothing trained):

\(s\) Mixing rate 0.5 0.0025 1.0 0.0500 2.0 0.2025 4.0 0.4300

Figure 3 — Mixing rate vs. \(s\). It climbs from essentially zero to 43% as the clouds spread.

From which scale can the clouds no longer be separated by straight lines? From \(s = 2\) onward. At \(s = 0.5\) and \(s = 1\) the mixing rate is tiny (0.25% and 5%), so a set of straight-line boundaries still separates the classes with only marginal error; at \(s = 2\) the mixing rate jumps to ~20% and the clouds visibly interpenetrate in Figure 2, so no set of straight lines can cleanly separate them. What happens to the smallest \(r_{ij}\) there? It falls below 1 — \(r_{01} = 0.663\) at \(s = 2\) — meaning the gap between the two closest centers is now smaller than the sum of their average spreads: the two clouds overlap by construction.

docs.title: C — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Overlap at \(s = 1\), and linear separability. In the original dataset the four clouds are mostly distinct, but Classes 0 and 1 overlap along the \(x_1 \approx 3\)–\(6\) band (their \(r_{01} = 1.326\) is the smallest ratio), and Class 1 brushes Class 2 near the bottom. Class 3 sits far to the right, cleanly apart. A single linear boundary cannot separate all four classes: one hyperplane only cuts the plane into two half-planes, and we have four regions. A set of linear boundaries, however, can — the 5% mixing rate at \(s = 1\) shows the classes are almost linearly separable, so a small number of straight cuts (or the piecewise-linear boundaries an MLP learns) does the job with little error.

2. Sketched decision boundaries. A trained network would carve the plane into one region per class. The nearest-mean (Voronoi) partition is a good sketch of what those piecewise-linear boundaries look like:

Sketched decision boundaries — the nearest-centroid partition at \(s = 1\). Each region is bounded by straight segments; only the handful of points on the wrong side of the Class 0 / Class 1 border are misclassified.

3. Relation to item B. As the clouds spread (larger \(s\)), the region where the network necessarily makes mistakes — the zone where two classes' points genuinely overlap — grows. The boundaries barely move (the means are fixed), but more points cross to the wrong side of them: this is precisely the mixing rate rising from 0.25% at \(s = 0.5\) to 43% at \(s = 4\) in Figure 3. Beyond \(s \approx 2\), where \(r_{01} < 1\), the overlap is unavoidable for any boundary, straight or curved: the irreducible (Bayes) error region widens with the spread.

docs.title: Non-Linearity in Higher Dimensions
docs.text: My approach: build two 5-D, two-class datasets and contrast them. Dataset I separates the classes by location (a mean shift), so it is essentially linearly separable; Dataset II separates them by radius (concentric shells), so no hyperplane can separate it even though a single quadratic feature can. All numbers come from the notebook linked at the end.

docs.title: A — Dataset I: shifted Gaussians
docs.text: I drew 500 samples per class from multivariate normals: Class A at \(\mu_A = [0,0,0,0,0]\) and Class B at \(\mu_B = [1.5,1.5,1.5,1.5,1.5]\), with the given covariances. Class B has larger variances and a negative correlation between the first two features, whereas Class A's is positive. This yields a \((1000, 5)\) matrix.

docs.title: B — Dataset II: concentric shells
docs.text: I drew directions uniformly on the unit sphere of \(\mathbb{R}^5\) (\(v \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_5)\), then \(u = v/\Vert v \Vert\)) and scaled each by a random radius: Class C (core) with \(\rho \sim \mathcal{N}(2.0, 0.4)\) and Class D (shell) with \(\rho \sim \mathcal{N}(5.0, 0.4)\), so \(x = \rho \, u\). I read the second parameter as a standard deviation of \(0.4\). This also yields a \((1000, 5)\) matrix, but with radial rather than location structure.

docs.title: C — Visualize and compare
docs.text:
Figure 4 — PCA to 2D. Dataset I (left) splits cleanly along PC1; Dataset II (right) shows the core (green) buried inside the shell (purple) — a linear projection cannot pull them apart.

Explained variance of the first two components:

Dataset PC1 PC2 PC1 + PC2 I — shifted Gaussians 0.513 0.158 0.670 II — concentric shells 0.216 0.213 0.429

The 2D projection preserves the classification-relevant information far better for Dataset I: its largest direction of variance (PC1) coincides with the mean-shift direction, so the classes split left/right in Figure 4. Dataset II is roughly isotropic, so its variance is spread almost evenly across all five axes (hence only 0.429 in two of them), and — crucially — the discriminative signal is radial, which no linear axis captures, so the classes stay superimposed.

Distance between class centers (in 5D) and the radius histograms:

Dataset \(\Vert \mu_1 - \mu_2 \Vert\) I — shifted Gaussians 3.264 II — concentric shells 0.266

Figure 5 — Radius \(\Vert x \Vert\) per class. Dataset I overlaps; Dataset II is perfectly separated in radius (\(\approx 2\) vs. \(\approx 5\)) despite its class centers nearly coinciding.

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Coincident centers + separated radii. In Dataset II the class centers are essentially the same point (distance \(0.266\), versus \(3.264\) for Dataset I), yet the radius histograms are completely disjoint. A hyperplane separates by location — which side of a flat boundary a point falls on — but here both classes share the same center and are spherically symmetric, so no hyperplane can separate them. The signal lives in the distance from the origin, a quantity a linear boundary cannot see.

2. Why no linear boundary works, ever. For any hyperplane \(w \cdot x = b\), project the data onto \(w\): since \(x = \rho\,u\) with \(u\) uniform on the sphere, \(w \cdot x = \rho\,(w \cdot u)\), and \(w \cdot u\) is symmetric about \(0\) with the same shape for both classes — only rescaled by \(\rho\). So both classes project to zero-mean, overlapping distributions (the shell just has heavier tails), and any threshold \(b\) misclassifies a large fraction. More data cannot fix this: it is a structural property — the core is enclosed by the shell, and a linear model can only ever carve out a single half-space, never an "inside vs. outside."

3. Does a mixed PCA view prove inseparability? No. PCA is a linear transformation, so a projection in which the classes look mixed (Figure 4, right; only \(0.429\) variance retained) proves only that no linear view separates them — not that no function does. My own results confirm this: the same Dataset II is separated perfectly by a single quadratic feature, \(f(x) = \Vert x \Vert^2 = \sum_i x_i^2\). Thresholding at radius \(3.5\) (i.e. \(f(x) = 12.25\)) — "predict shell when \(\sum_i x_i^2 > 12.25\)" — gives accuracy \(1.0000\) on the 1000 points.

docs.title: Preparing Real-World Data for a Neural Network
docs.text: My approach: preprocess the Kaggle Spaceship Titanic dataset for a network with tanh hidden layers, which means every input must end up on a bounded, tanh-compatible scale. Crucially, every transformation statistic is fit on the training split only, so no test information leaks into the pipeline. (The data is train.csv; the notebook loads a local copy and falls back to a public mirror.)

docs.title: A — Get to know the data
docs.text:
Goal. Each row is a passenger; the target Transported is a boolean — whether the passenger was transported to another dimension during the spacetime anomaly. It is the binary label a classifier predicts. The classes are almost perfectly balanced: True = 0.5036, False = 0.4964.

Features (raw shape \((8693, 14)\)):

  • Numerical: Age, RoomService, FoodCourt, ShoppingMall, Spa, VRDeck
  • Categorical: HomePlanet, CryoSleep, Cabin, Destination, VIP, Name
  • Identifier (dropped): PassengerId

Missing values (every column is missing ~2%):

Column Missing count Missing % CryoSleep 217 2.50 ShoppingMall 208 2.39 VIP 203 2.34 HomePlanet 201 2.31 Name 200 2.30 Cabin 199 2.29 VRDeck 188 2.16 FoodCourt 183 2.11 Spa 183 2.11 Destination 182 2.09 RoomService 181 2.08 Age 179 2.06

Spending columns — mean, median, maximum (full dataset):

Column Mean Median Max RoomService 224.69 0.0 14327.0 FoodCourt 458.08 0.0 29813.0 ShoppingMall 173.73 0.0 23492.0 Spa 311.14 0.0 22408.0 VRDeck 304.85 0.0 24133.0

For every spending column the mean sits far above a median of 0: most passengers spend nothing while a few spend enormous amounts. That gap is the signature of a strongly right-skewed, heavy-tailed distribution — which is exactly what the \(\log(1+x)\) transform in item C is meant to tame.

docs.title: B — Split before you transform
docs.text: I split 80/20, stratified by Transported, with random_state=42 — giving a training set of \((6954, 13)\) and a test set of \((1739, 13)\). Why split first? Every statistic used to transform the data — the imputation medians, the most-frequent categories, and the min/max used for scaling — must be learned from the training set alone. Computing them on the full dataset and splitting afterwards would let information from the test rows bleed into the pipeline (data leakage), and the reported performance would be optimistically biased and untrustworthy.

docs.title: C — Preprocess
docs.text:
1. Missing data. Numerical columns (Age + the five spending columns) are imputed with the median — robust to the heavy right tails, so a handful of big spenders cannot drag the fill value upward. Categorical columns (HomePlanet, CryoSleep, Destination, VIP) are imputed with the most frequent category. Both imputers are fit on the training set and only applied to the test set; after imputation there are 0 remaining NaN in the columns used.

2. Categorical encoding. I one-hot encode the four categoricals with OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), fit on the training categories. A category that appears only in the test set is encoded as all-zeros across that feature's columns rather than raising an error, so the pipeline never breaks on an unseen value. This yields 10 columns: HomePlanet (3), CryoSleep (2), Destination (3), VIP (2).

3. Feature engineering. I create TotalSpend, the sum of the five spending columns, and drop Cabin, Name, and PassengerId (free-text / identifiers with no direct numerical meaning).

4. Heavy tails. I apply \(\log(1+x)\) to the five spending columns and TotalSpend. This compresses the long tail into a roughly symmetric range. It helps a tanh network because the raw values (up to ~30 000) would instantly saturate tanh at \(\pm 1\), where its gradient is ~0 and learning stalls; log1p also maps \(0 \mapsto 0\), keeping the many zero-spenders well behaved.

5. Scaling. I normalize the continuous columns to \([-1, 1]\) with MinMaxScaler, fit on the training set. I chose normalization over standardization because it directly matches the output range of tanh, so no input starts in the saturated region; together with the 0/1 one-hot columns, the whole matrix lives inside \([-1, 1]\). After scaling, the training matrix spans exactly \([-1.000, 1.000]\); the test matrix spans \([-1.000, 1.138]\) — slightly above 1 because the scaler was fit on the training range and a test value exceeds it (the correct, leakage-free behavior; tanh still handles it gracefully).

docs.title: D — Verify and visualize
docs.text:
Figure 6 — FoodCourt before (raw, imputed: a spike at 0 with a long tail to ~30 000) and after \(\log(1+x)\) + scaling to \([-1, 1]\) (zero-spenders at \(-1\), the rest spread across the range).

Final checks. No remaining NaN in either feature matrix; the final training feature matrix has shape \((6954, 17)\) (7 continuous + 10 one-hot columns); and the value range is tanh-compatible — train \([-1.000, 1.000]\), test \([-1.000, 1.138]\).

Which decision most affects training? The \(\log(1+x)\) transform on the spending columns. Without it, those features carry raw values up to ~30 000; once scaled they would collapse almost every passenger onto a tiny cluster near \(-1\) while a few outliers pin the extreme, so tanh would saturate and the spending signal — which is highly predictive of Transported — would contribute almost no usable gradient. The log transform is what turns those columns into a well-spread, learnable input (visible in Figure 6).

def mixing_rate(points):
    dists = np.linalg.norm(points[:, None, :] - MEANS[None, :, :], axis=2)
    return float(np.mean(dists.argmin(axis=1) != LABELS))

docs.text: Runnable code for the Data deliverable. This notebook generates the four Gaussian clouds, studies how a global spread factor changes their separability, and saves every figure the report shows. All randomness comes from a single fixed generator (rng = np.random.default_rng(42)) so the results are reproducible.

docs.title: A — Generate the clouds¶
docs.text: 400 samples, 100 per class, one Gaussian per class with the given per-axis means and standard deviations. Figure 1 is the scatter at $s = 1$ with the class means marked.

docs.title: B — More or less spread out¶
docs.text: The same four classes regenerated at $s \in \{0.5, 1, 2, 4\}$ — means fixed, only the spread scaled. Figure 2 plots them on shared axes so the comparison is honest.

docs.title: Separation ratios $r_{ij}$ at $s = 1$¶
docs.text: $r_{ij} = \Vert \mu_i - \mu_j \Vert / (\bar{\sigma}_i + \bar{\sigma}_j)$, with $\bar{\sigma}_k = (\sigma_{k,x} + \sigma_{k,y})/2$. High means well separated; low means blending.

docs.title: Mixing rate per scale¶
docs.text: Fraction of points whose nearest class mean is not their own class — a purely geometric check against the four fixed means, nothing trained. Figure 3 plots it against $s$.

docs.title: C — Analysis: sketched decision boundaries¶
docs.text: A trained network carves the plane into one region per class. The nearest-centroid (Voronoi) partition is a good sketch of those piecewise-linear boundaries.

docs.title: Exercise 2 — Non-Linearity in Higher Dimensions¶
docs.text: Runnable code for the Data deliverable. Two 5-dimensional, two-class datasets are contrasted: Dataset I (two shifted multivariate Gaussians) is essentially linearly separable, while Dataset II (two concentric spherical shells) is not separable by any hyperplane even though it is trivially separable by radius. All randomness comes from a single fixed generator so the results are reproducible.

docs.title: A — Dataset I: shifted Gaussians¶
docs.text: 500 samples per class from multivariate normals with the given means and covariances. Class A is centered at the origin; Class B is shifted to $[1.5]^5$ and has larger variances and a negative correlation between the first two features (Class A's is positive).

docs.title: B — Dataset II: concentric shells¶
docs.text: Directions drawn uniformly on the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^5$ ($v \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_5)$, then $u = v / \Vert v \Vert$), scaled by a random radius. Class C is the inner core (radius $\approx 2$), Class D the outer shell (radius $\approx 5$). I read $\mathcal{N}(\mu, 0.4)$ as standard deviation $0.4$.

docs.title: Figure 4 — PCA projection to 2D¶
docs.text: PCA is fit on each full dataset (both classes) and used to project to the first two principal components.

docs.title: Distance between class centers, and Figure 5 (radius histograms)¶
docs.text: Both computed in the full 5D space.

docs.title: D — Analysis: a function that separates Dataset II¶
docs.text: PCA (a linear map) mixes the two shells, yet a single quadratic feature $f(x) = \Vert x \Vert^2 = \sum_i x_i^2$ separates them cleanly. With classes at radius $\approx 2$ and $\approx 5$, the natural threshold sits at radius $3.5$, i.e. $f(x) = 3.5^2 = 12.25$.

docs.title: Exercise 3 — Preparing Real-World Data for a Neural Network¶
docs.text: Runnable code for the Data deliverable. The Spaceship Titanic dataset is preprocessed for a network whose hidden layers use tanh, so the inputs are put on a bounded, tanh-compatible scale. Every statistic used in a transformation (median, most-frequent category, min/max) is fit only on the training split to avoid data leakage.

docs.title: A — Get to know the data¶
docs.text: Goal. Each row is a passenger; the target Transported is a boolean — whether the passenger was transported to another dimension during the spacetime-anomaly incident. It is the binary label a classifier must predict.

docs.title: B — Split before you transform¶
docs.text: Stratified 80/20 split with a fixed seed. Why split first? Every statistic used to transform the data — imputation medians, the most-frequent category, and the min/max used for scaling — must be learned from the training set only. If they were computed on the full dataset and split afterwards, information from the test rows would leak into the training pipeline and the reported performance would be optimistic and untrustworthy.

docs.title: 1. Missing data¶
docs.text:
• Numerical (Age + the five spending columns): impute with the median — robust to the heavy right tails, so a few big spenders do not drag the fill value.
  • Categorical (HomePlanet, CryoSleep, Destination, VIP): impute with the most frequent category.

Both imputers are fit on the training set and merely applied to the test set.

docs.title: 2. Categorical encoding (one-hot)¶
docs.text: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") is fit on the training categories. A category that appears only in the test set is encoded as all-zeros across that feature's columns instead of raising an error, so the pipeline never breaks on an unseen value.

docs.title: 3. Feature engineering — TotalSpend¶
docs.text: Sum of the five spending columns. Cabin, Name, and PassengerId are dropped (free-text / identifiers with no direct numerical meaning for the network).

docs.title: 4. Heavy tails — $\log(1+x)$¶
docs.text: The spending columns (and TotalSpend) are right-skewed, so I apply $\log(1+x)$. This compresses the long tail into a roughly symmetric range: without it, the huge raw values would saturate tanh (pushing it to $\pm 1$ where its gradient vanishes), stalling learning. log1p also maps $0 \mapsto 0$, keeping the many zero-spenders well behaved.

docs.title: 5. Scaling — Normalization to $[-1, 1]$¶
docs.text: I normalize the continuous columns to $[-1, 1]$ with MinMaxScaler, fit on the training set. This directly matches the output range of tanh, so no input sits in the activation's saturated region from the start; combined with the 0/1 one-hot columns, the whole feature matrix lives inside $[-1, 1]$.

docs.title: MLP — Understanding Multi-Layer Perceptrons
docs.text:
Approach. Exercise 1 is one step of backpropagation worked by hand. For Exercises 2–4 I wrote a single MLP class from scratch in mlp.py (NumPy only). The layer sizes, the output activation (sigmoid or softmax) and the matching loss (binary or categorical cross-entropy) are constructor arguments. The forward pass, the backward pass and the update step are the same code for the binary problem (Exercise 2), the 3-class problem (Exercise 3) and the deeper network (Exercise 4).

Technical rules used throughout: a single fixed generator rng = np.random.default_rng(42); every plot has a title, axis labels and a legend; scikit-learn is used only for make_blobs, make_classification, train_test_split, the confusion matrix and the logistic-regression baselines. Activations, losses, gradients and updates are my own code.

docs.title: Exercise 1 — One Step of Backpropagation, by Hand
docs.text:
Network: 2 inputs, 2 hidden \(\tanh\) units, 1 \(\tanh\) output, loss \(L = (y-\hat{y})^2\). Values: \(\mathbf{x} = [0.5, -0.2]\), \(y = 1\), \(\eta = 0.3\), and

\[ \mathbf{W}^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & -0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b}^{(1)} = [0.1,\ -0.2], \quad \mathbf{W}^{(2)} = [0.5,\ -0.3], \quad b^{(2)} = 0.2 \]

docs.title: B — Backward pass
docs.text:
Start. Differentiating the loss with respect to the output:

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} = -2(y - \hat{y}) = -2(0.632753) = -1.265507 \]

1. Through the output \(\tanh\). Using \(\tanh'(u) = 1 - \tanh^2(u) = 1 - \hat{y}^2\):

\[ 1 - \hat{y}^2 = 1 - 0.367247^2 = 0.865130, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^{(2)}} = -1.265507 \times 0.865130 = -1.094828 \]

2. Output layer. Because \(u^{(2)} = \mathbf{W}^{(2)} \mathbf{h}^{(1)} + b^{(2)}\), the derivative of \(u^{(2)}\) with respect to each weight is the matching hidden activation, and with respect to the bias it is 1:

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(2)}} &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^{(2)}}\, \mathbf{h}^{(1)} = -1.094828 \times [0.263625,\ -0.178081] = [-0.288624,\ 0.194968] \\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}} &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^{(2)}} = -1.094828 \end{aligned} \]

3. Propagate back. The derivative of \(u^{(2)}\) with respect to \(\mathbf{h}^{(1)}\) is \(\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\). The derivative of \(\mathbf{h}^{(1)}\) with respect to \(\mathbf{z}^{(1)}\) is \(1 - (\mathbf{h}^{(1)})^2\), applied element-wise:

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{h}^{(1)}} &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^{(2)}}\, \mathbf{W}^{(2)} = -1.094828 \times [0.5,\ -0.3] = [-0.547414,\ 0.328448] \\ 1 - (\mathbf{h}^{(1)})^2 &= [1 - 0.263625^2,\ 1 - 0.178081^2] = [0.930502,\ 0.968287] \\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(1)}} &= [-0.547414 \times 0.930502,\ 0.328448 \times 0.968287] = [-0.509370,\ 0.318032] \end{aligned} \]

4. Hidden layer. Because \(\mathbf{z}^{(1)} = \mathbf{W}^{(1)} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}\), the weight gradient is the outer product of the hidden gradient with the input, and the bias gradient equals the hidden gradient:

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(1)}}\, \mathbf{x}^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.509370 \times 0.5 & -0.509370 \times (-0.2) \\ 0.318032 \times 0.5 & 0.318032 \times (-0.2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.254685 & 0.101874 \\ 0.159016 & -0.063606 \end{bmatrix} \] \[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(1)}} = [-0.509370,\ 0.318032] \]

docs.title: C — Parameter update
docs.text:
Each parameter moves by \(-\eta\) times its gradient, with \(\eta = 0.3\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{W}^{(2)} &\leftarrow [0.5 - 0.3(-0.288624),\ -0.3 - 0.3(0.194968)] = [0.586587,\ -0.358490] \\ b^{(2)} &\leftarrow 0.2 - 0.3(-1.094828) = 0.528448 \\ \mathbf{W}^{(1)} &\leftarrow \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 - 0.3(-0.254685) & -0.1 - 0.3(0.101874) \\ 0.2 - 0.3(0.159016) & 0.4 - 0.3(-0.063606) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.376405 & -0.130562 \\ 0.152295 & 0.419082 \end{bmatrix} \\ \mathbf{b}^{(1)} &\leftarrow [0.1 - 0.3(-0.509370),\ -0.2 - 0.3(0.318032)] = [0.252811,\ -0.295410] \end{aligned} \]

Would the loss go up or down on a second forward pass? Down. Gradient descent moves every parameter against its gradient, which is the direction of steepest local decrease of \(L\). With a step this size the decrease is real, not just in theory. Rerunning the forward pass with the updated parameters gives \(\hat{y} = 0.711181\) and \(L = 0.083417\), against \(L = 0.400377\) before the update. The output moved from 0.367 toward the target 1.0. The biggest changes are in \(b^{(2)}\) and \(\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\), which sit closest to the loss and have the largest gradients.

The notebook code/ex1_backprop.ipynb repeats these calculations in NumPy as a check, and every number above matches.

docs.title: A — Generate the data
docs.text:
The data is generated exactly as specified: make_blobs with centers \((0,0)\), \((3,3)\) and \((-3,-3)\), 500/250/250 points, cluster_std=1.2, random_state=42, and y = (c > 0). Class 0 is the central cluster; Class 1 is split into the two outer clusters on either side of it. The split is 80/20 (test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y), giving 800 training points and 200 test points.

docs.title: C — Implement the MLP
docs.text:
The class below is the whole model and is reused unchanged in Exercises 3 and 4:

  • Layers: layer_sizes is a list such as [2, 8, 1], so any depth works. Weights are drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1/n_{\text{in}})\) using the shared rng, and biases start at zero.
  • Forward pass: \(\tanh\) on every hidden layer; sigmoid (binary) or softmax (multi-class) at the output.
  • Loss: binary cross-entropy (Exercise 2) or categorical cross-entropy (Exercise 3).
  • Backward pass: the output error is (P - Y) / N. Each layer's weight gradient is A[l].T @ delta and its bias gradient is the column sum of delta. The error is sent back with delta @ W[l].T, multiplied by the \(\tanh\) derivative 1 - A[l]**2.
  • Update: full-batch gradient descent, \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \nabla_\theta L\).

I checked the analytic gradients against finite differences for both output types, and they agree.

"""A multi-layer perceptron written from scratch with NumPy.

Hidden layers use tanh. The output layer is either a sigmoid (binary, paired
with binary cross-entropy) or a softmax (multi-class, paired with categorical
cross-entropy). Both pairs give the same output gradient, dL/du = (p - y) / N,
so the forward pass, backward pass, and update below are shared verbatim by
every exercise; only the output activation and the loss are arguments.
"""

import numpy as np

EPS = 1e-12


def sigmoid(u):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-u))


def softmax(u):
    e = np.exp(u - u.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))  # shift for numerical stability
    return e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)


def binary_cross_entropy(p, y):
    """L = -mean[y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p)]; p and y have shape (N, 1)."""
    p = np.clip(p, EPS, 1 - EPS)  # avoid log(0)
    return float(-np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p)))


def categorical_cross_entropy(p, y):
    """L = -mean over samples of sum_k y_k log p_k; y is one-hot, shape (N, K)."""
    p = np.clip(p, EPS, 1.0)  # avoid log(0)
    return float(-np.mean(np.sum(y * np.log(p), axis=1)))


OUTPUTS = {
    "sigmoid": (sigmoid, binary_cross_entropy),
    "softmax": (softmax, categorical_cross_entropy),
}


class MLP:
    """Fully connected network; ``layer_sizes`` = [n_in, hidden..., n_out]."""

    def __init__(self, layer_sizes, rng, output="sigmoid"):
        self.layer_sizes = list(layer_sizes)
        self.output = output
        self.out_act, self.loss_fn = OUTPUTS[output]
        # Weights ~ N(0, 1/fan_in) keep tanh pre-activations out of saturation.
        self.W = [rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(n_in), size=(n_in, n_out))
                  for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:])]
        self.b = [np.zeros(n_out) for n_out in layer_sizes[1:]]

    def n_params(self):
        return int(sum(W.size + b.size for W, b in zip(self.W, self.b)))

    def encode(self, y):
        """Integer labels -> targets shaped like the network output."""
        if self.output == "sigmoid":
            return y.reshape(-1, 1).astype(float)
        return np.eye(self.layer_sizes[-1])[y]

    def forward(self, X):
        """Returns output probabilities and every layer's activation."""
        A = [X]  # A[l] is the input to layer l; backward needs all of them
        for W, b in zip(self.W[:-1], self.b[:-1]):
            A.append(np.tanh(A[-1] @ W + b))  # hidden layer: h = tanh(A W + b)
        P = self.out_act(A[-1] @ self.W[-1] + self.b[-1])  # sigmoid or softmax
        return P, A

    def backward(self, A, P, Y):
        """Gradients of the mean loss w.r.t. every weight and bias."""
        delta = (P - Y) / len(Y)  # dL/du at the output (sigmoid+BCE or softmax+CCE)
        grads_W, grads_b = [None] * len(self.W), [None] * len(self.b)
        for l in reversed(range(len(self.W))):
            grads_W[l] = A[l].T @ delta    # dL/dW = (layer input)^T . (error at its output)
            grads_b[l] = delta.sum(axis=0)  # dL/db = error summed over the batch
            if l > 0:
                # back through W^(l), then through tanh: d tanh = 1 - tanh^2
                delta = (delta @ self.W[l].T) * (1.0 - A[l] ** 2)
        return grads_W, grads_b

    def update(self, grads_W, grads_b, lr):
        """Gradient descent step: theta <- theta - lr * dL/dtheta."""
        for l in range(len(self.W)):
            self.W[l] -= lr * grads_W[l]
            self.b[l] -= lr * grads_b[l]

    def fit(self, X, y, epochs, lr):
        """Full-batch gradient descent; returns the training loss per epoch."""
        Y = self.encode(y)
        losses = []
        for _ in range(epochs):
            P, A = self.forward(X)
            losses.append(self.loss_fn(P, Y))
            grads_W, grads_b = self.backward(A, P, Y)
            self.update(grads_W, grads_b, lr)
        return losses

    def predict(self, X):
        P, _ = self.forward(X)
        if self.output == "sigmoid":
            return (P[:, 0] >= 0.5).astype(int)
        return P.argmax(axis=1)

    def accuracy(self, X, y):
        return float(np.mean(self.predict(X) == y))

Training. Architecture [2, 8, 1] (2 inputs, one hidden layer of 8 tanh units, 1 sigmoid output; 33 parameters), learning rate \(\eta = 0.5\), 2000 epochs of full-batch gradient descent. The final training loss is 0.1043, the training accuracy is 0.9675, and the test accuracy is 0.9150.

Figure 2 — Binary cross-entropy on the training set at each epoch. It falls quickly in the first few hundred epochs and then levels off near 0.10.

Figure 3 — The network's prediction on a grid, with the test points on top. Blue is the Class 0 region and red is the Class 1 region. The Class 0 region is a diagonal band through the middle; Class 1 gets both corners outside it.

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
A logistic regression draws one straight line and labels one side Class 0 and the other side Class 1. Figure 3 shows the region Class 1 actually needs. It is two separate pieces: the bottom-left corner around \((-3,-3)\) and the top-right corner around \((3,3)\), with the Class 0 band running between them. Any straight line gives Class 1 a single half-plane, so it can contain at most one of the two corners. The other corner has to share a side with Class 0.

The best a straight line can do, then, is find Class 0 plus roughly one of the outer clusters. Because Class 0 sits in the middle and the two Class 1 clusters are symmetric about it, the log-loss gains from leaning toward either corner cancel out. Logistic regression settles on a nearly useless line that mixes the classes on both sides, and it scores 47.5%, worse than a constant guess.

The hidden layer fixes this. Each of the 8 tanh units makes its own soft line, and the output unit combines them. Two roughly parallel lines, one on each side of the center, are enough to carve out the band in Figure 3: inside both lines means Class 0, and outside either line means Class 1. That non-convex, two-piece Class 1 region is something no single line can make. The remaining errors (test 91.5%) are points in the overlap where the clusters touch, since cluster_std = 1.2 makes some outer points fall inside the band.

docs.title: B — Adapt the network
docs.text:
Only two things change, and both are constructor arguments: the output layer has 3 units, and output="softmax" selects softmax plus categorical cross-entropy. forward, backward and update are the same code, unchanged, as Exercise 2. The labels are one-hot encoded by encode.

Deriving the gradient for softmax with cross-entropy. For one sample with logits \(u_1, \dots, u_K\), the probabilities and the loss are

\[ p_k = \frac{e^{u_k}}{\sum_{j} e^{u_j}}, \qquad L = -\sum_{k} y_k \log p_k \]

where \(\mathbf{y}\) is one-hot, so \(\sum_k y_k = 1\). First, the derivative of softmax. Each \(p_k\) depends on every logit:

\[ \frac{\partial p_k}{\partial u_i} = p_k(\delta_{ki} - p_i) \]

where \(\delta_{ki}\) is 1 if \(k = i\) and 0 otherwise. Then apply the chain rule through the loss, using \(\partial L / \partial p_k = -y_k / p_k\):

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial u_i} = \sum_k \left(-\frac{y_k}{p_k}\right) p_k(\delta_{ki} - p_i) = -\sum_k y_k \delta_{ki} + p_i \sum_k y_k = -y_i + p_i \] \[ \boxed{\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{u}} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}} \]

The \(p_k\) from the softmax derivative cancels the \(1/p_k\) from the logarithm. The result is just "prediction minus target". This is the same form as sigmoid with binary cross-entropy in Exercise 2, which also gives \(p - y\). That is why one backward pass works for both: backward starts from delta = (P - Y) / N, and nothing about the number of classes appears anywhere else. This is the verbatim reuse the extra point asks for.

docs.title: C — Train and evaluate
docs.text:
Architecture [4, 16, 3] (4 inputs, one hidden layer of 16 tanh units, 3 softmax outputs; 131 parameters), learning rate \(\eta = 0.5\), 2000 epochs of full-batch gradient descent, initialized with default_rng(42). The final training loss is 0.2597, the training accuracy is 0.9050, and the test accuracy is 0.8567.

Figure 4 — Categorical cross-entropy on the training set at each epoch. It drops steeply at first and is still creeping down at epoch 2000, ending at 0.2597.

Figure 5 — Confusion matrix on the 300 test points (rows are true classes, columns are predicted classes). The diagonal holds 90, 77 and 90 correct predictions.

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
The most-confused pair is Class 0 and Class 1, with 18 test errors between them (12 Class 1 points predicted as Class 0, and 6 the other way). Class 1 and Class 2 come next with 16 errors, and Class 0 and Class 2 have only 9. Class 1 is the weak class overall: it has 77 correct out of 100, while the other two have 90 each. Of its 23 errors, 12 go to Class 0 and 11 go to Class 2.

An explanation from the cluster structure. make_classification places 6 Gaussian clusters (2 per class) at vertices of a hypercube in the 4-D informative space. With class_sep=1.0 the vertices are close relative to the unit-variance clusters. Because each class is two clusters at random vertices, a class is not one compact blob. It is two blobs that can sit on opposite sides of another class's cluster. One of Class 1's clusters evidently sits next to a Class 0 cluster, and the other next to a Class 2 cluster. Points in the region where two clusters overlap are genuinely ambiguous, so no boundary can fix them. That is why Class 1's errors split almost evenly between its two neighbors.

Baseline. Logistic regression (multinomial, linear boundaries) reaches 0.6633 on the same split. The hidden layer adds about 19 percentage points (0.6633 to 0.8567). A linear model gives each class one convex region, but each class here consists of two clusters that need not lie on the same side of any hyperplane. The hidden units can build a region that wraps around both of a class's clusters, which a linear model cannot do.

docs.title: Exercise 4 — Does a Second Hidden Layer Help?
A — Train the deeper network
docs.text: Architecture [4, 16, 16, 3]: two hidden layers of 16 tanh units each, and 403 parameters. It uses the same data, the same split, \(\eta = 0.5\) and 2000 epochs, exactly as in Exercise 3, and the same MLP class with only layer_sizes changed. With seed 42 it reaches a test accuracy of 0.8533, compared with 0.8567 for the 1-hidden-layer network on the same seed. Averaged over three seeds it reaches 0.8522.

docs.title: B — Compare
docs.text:
Both networks were trained with default_rng(seed) for seeds 42, 43 and 44. The seed sets the weight initialization; the data and split are fixed. Each figure below is the mean over the 3 seeds:

hidden layers parameters final train loss test accuracy Exercise 3 [4, 16, 3] 1 131 0.2617 0.8489 Exercise 4 [4, 16, 16, 3] 2 403 0.1727 0.8522

Per seed, test accuracy for the 1-hidden-layer network was 0.8567, 0.8367 and 0.8533, and for the 2-hidden-layer network it was 0.8533, 0.8467 and 0.8567. The mean difference (Exercise 4 minus Exercise 3) is +0.0033, which is one test point out of 300.

Figure 6 — Training loss on a log scale. Faint lines are individual seeds and the thick lines are the means over 3 seeds. The deeper network (purple) drives the training loss much lower but shows occasional spikes; the shallow network (green) decreases smoothly.

docs.title: C — Analysis
docs.text:
The second layer did not meaningfully help. On training loss the deeper network wins clearly: 0.1727 against 0.2617, about a third lower. On test accuracy the two are tied: +0.0033 on average, smaller than the spread between seeds of the same model (0.8367 to 0.8567 for the shallow one). The training loss and the test accuracy tell different stories. The extra capacity was spent fitting the training set more tightly, not on finding structure that carries over to new data.

Why, from the structure of the data. The data is 6 Gaussian clusters in 4-D, and each class is the union of 2 of them. The ideal boundary is a handful of roughly flat pieces separating neighboring clusters. One hidden layer of 16 tanh units already gives 16 soft hyperplanes, more than enough to surround 6 blobs. The test errors that remain come from points in the overlap between clusters, and no network can classify those correctly from these 4 features. Extra depth cannot create information that is not in the data, so the accuracy ceiling is set by the cluster overlap, not by model capacity.

What depth costs. The second layer triples the parameters (131 to 403), and the gradient must pass through one more \(\tanh\) Jacobian. Figure 6 shows the cost in optimization: with the same \(\eta = 0.5\), the deeper network's loss spikes several times (near epochs 320, 400 and 850) before recovering. The shallow network never does. With 4 hidden-layer multiplications instead of 2 in the backward pass, the same step size is close to too large for the deeper network. Its lower training loss with no accuracy gain is the usual sign of extra capacity being used to memorize the 1200 training points.

What data would reward depth. A second layer pays off when the target is a composition of features, not just a union of a few blobs. Examples are hierarchical structure such as images (edges, then parts, then objects), functions like parity or XOR in many dimensions that a shallow network can only represent with exponentially many units, or tightly interleaved manifolds such as spirals with many turns. On data like that, a shallow network would need far more units to match a deep one, and the deeper network's lower training loss would carry over to the test set. That data should also be large enough that the extra parameters are not just memorizing.

docs.title: Mlp
Perceptron — Understanding Perceptrons and Their Limitations
docs.text:
Approach. I wrote a single-layer perceptron from scratch in perceptron.py (NumPy only — no scikit-learn model) as one reusable class: the step activation, the {0,1} error-driven update, and a training loop with an optional pocket. The same class trains both a separable dataset (Exercise 1), where it converges to 100%, and a non-separable one (Exercise 2), where it cannot and the pocket algorithm keeps the best-so-far weights. The main subtlety was matching the update rule to {0,1} labels (not the ±1 textbook form) and using a non-zero weight initialization so the learning-rate study in item D is meaningful.

Technical rules used throughout: a single fixed generator rng = np.random.default_rng(42); every plot has a title, axis labels, and a class legend; only numpy, pandas, matplotlib/seaborn are used, and the perceptron is entirely my own code.

docs.title: A — Generate the data
docs.text:
Two 2-D Gaussian clouds, 1000 points each: Class 0 \(\sim \mathcal{N}([1.5,1.5], 0.5 I)\) and Class 1 \(\sim \mathcal{N}([5,5], 0.5 I)\). The centers are ~5 units apart while the per-axis standard deviation is only \(\sqrt{0.5} \approx 0.71\), so the clouds are linearly separable.

Figure 1 — 2000 points, one color per class. The two clouds are cleanly apart.

docs.title: B — Implement the perceptron
docs.text:
The model is written from scratch and reused unchanged in Exercise 2:

  • Prediction: \(\hat{y} = \mathrm{step}(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b)\), with \(\mathrm{step}(z)=1\) if \(z\ge 0\) else \(0\).
  • Update (matched to \(\{0,1\}\) labels): \(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta\,(y-\hat{y})\,\mathbf{x}\), \(b \leftarrow b + \eta\,(y-\hat{y})\). The error \((y-\hat{y})\) is \(0\) on a correct prediction, so only mistakes trigger an update.
  • Init: \(\mathbf{w}\sim\) rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2), \(b=0\) (non-zero, see D.3).
  • Learning rate: \(\eta = 0.01\).
  • Stopping: a full pass with no update, or 100 epochs; accuracy recorded each epoch.
"""A single-layer perceptron written from scratch (no third-party model).

The activation, prediction, update rule, and training loop are all implemented
here with NumPy only. The same class is reused for both exercises; Exercise 2
turns on the ``pocket`` flag to keep the best-so-far weights on non-separable
data.
"""

import numpy as np


def step(z):
    """Heaviside step: 1 if z >= 0 else 0 (works on scalars or arrays)."""
    return (z >= 0).astype(int)


class Perceptron:
    """Perceptron with the {0, 1} error-driven update rule.

    Prediction:  y_hat = step(w . x + b)
    Update:      w <- w + eta * (y - y_hat) * x
                 b <- b + eta * (y - y_hat)
    """

    def __init__(self, n_features, rng, lr=0.01):
        # Non-zero init: from w = 0 the learning rate only rescales w (see D.3),
        # so we draw small random weights instead.
        self.w = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=n_features)
        self.b = 0.0
        self.lr = float(lr)

    def predict(self, X):
        """Vectorised prediction for a matrix of samples (n, n_features)."""
        return step(X @ self.w + self.b)

    def accuracy(self, X, y):
        return float(np.mean(self.predict(X) == y))

    def train(self, X, y, max_epochs=100, pocket=False):
        """Train until a full pass produces no update, or max_epochs.

        Returns a history dict (per-epoch accuracy, best-so-far accuracy, and
        update count) and the pocket record (best weights, bias, accuracy, and
        the epoch at which the best occurred).
        """
        n = len(y)
        best = {
            "w": self.w.copy(),
            "b": self.b,
            "acc": self.accuracy(X, y),
            "epoch": 0,
        }
        history = {"acc": [], "best_acc": [], "updates": []}

        for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
            updates = 0
            for i in range(n):
                xi, yi = X[i], y[i]
                y_hat = 1 if (self.w @ xi + self.b) >= 0 else 0
                error = yi - y_hat            # 0 if correct, +/-1 on a mistake
                if error != 0:
                    self.w = self.w + self.lr * error * xi
                    self.b = self.b + self.lr * error
                    updates += 1
                    if pocket:
                        acc = self.accuracy(X, y)
                        if acc > best["acc"]:
                            best = {
                                "w": self.w.copy(),
                                "b": self.b,
                                "acc": acc,
                                "epoch": epoch,
                            }

            history["acc"].append(self.accuracy(X, y))
            history["best_acc"].append(best["acc"])
            history["updates"].append(updates)

            if updates == 0:      # a clean pass: the data is separated
                break

        return history, best

docs.text:
Training converged in 26 epochs to 100% accuracy, with final weights \(\mathbf{w} = [0.0505,\ 0.0289]\) and bias \(b = -0.25\).

Figure 2 — The learned boundary \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b=0\) cleanly separates the clouds; 0 points are misclassified.

Figure 3 — Accuracy climbs (with oscillations, since a single update can shift the boundary) and locks at 1.0 by epoch 25–26, after which a clean pass stops training.

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Why separable data converges quickly. The update fires only on mistakes (\(y-\hat{y}=0\) means no change). As the boundary moves into the gap between the clouds, fewer points are misclassified, so the number of updates per epoch falls toward zero; once a full pass makes no mistake, the stopping condition triggers. The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees this happens in a finite number of updates for separable data — here, 26 epochs.

2. Learning-rate comparison (\(\eta=0.01\) vs \(\eta=1.0\)). Same data, same initialization, only \(\eta\) changed:

\(\eta\) epochs final acc \(\mathbf{w}\) \(b\) \(\mathbf{w}/\Vert\mathbf{w}\Vert\) 0.01 26 1.0000 \([0.0505, 0.0289]\) \(-0.25\) \([0.8681, 0.4963]\) 1.0 37 1.0000 \([5.871, 3.359]\) \(-31.0\) \([0.8679, 0.4967]\)

Both reach 100%. The two weight directions are essentially identical (cosine similarity \(1.0000\), angle \(0.02^\circ\)), but the magnitudes differ by ~100× — exactly the ratio of the learning rates. This is the point of the hint: every update adds \(\eta\,\mathbf{x}\) to weights that started at magnitude ~0.01, so with \(\eta=1.0\) the accumulated updates (\(\approx \eta\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert \approx 5\) per step) instantly dwarf the tiny init and \(\Vert\mathbf{w}\Vert\) grows to ~6.8, whereas with \(\eta=0.01\) it stays ~0.06. Because the boundary \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b=0\) is invariant to the overall scale of \((\mathbf{w},b)\), the two lines share the same orientation; they differ only in their offset \(-b/\Vert\mathbf{w}\Vert\) (\(\approx 4.30\) vs \(4.58\)), i.e. they sit at slightly different places within the separating margin — both valid. So \(\eta\) controls the scale of the weights and where in the margin the boundary lands (and the epoch count), not the final orientation on cleanly separable data.

3. Why a zero start would make \(\eta\) irrelevant. Start from \(\mathbf{w}_0=\mathbf{0},\ b_0=0\) and run training at rate \(\eta\). Claim: at every step \(t\), \(\mathbf{w}^{(\eta)}_t = \eta\,\mathbf{a}_t\) and \(b^{(\eta)}_t = \eta\,c_t\) for rate-independent \(\mathbf{a}_t, c_t\). By induction: it holds at \(t=0\) (both sides zero). The prediction is \(\hat{y} = \mathrm{step}(\mathbf{w}_t\cdot\mathbf{x}+b_t) = \mathrm{step}(\eta(\mathbf{a}_t\cdot\mathbf{x}+c_t)) = \mathrm{step}(\mathbf{a}_t\cdot\mathbf{x}+c_t)\) because \(\eta>0\) does not change a sign. So \(\hat{y}\) — and therefore the error \((y-\hat{y})\) — is identical for every \(\eta\). The update then gives \(\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \eta\,\mathbf{a}_t + \eta(y-\hat{y})\mathbf{x} = \eta\,\mathbf{a}_{t+1}\), closing the induction. Hence running with \(\eta_1\) and \(\eta_2\) yields weights that differ only by the constant factor \(\eta_2/\eta_1\); the decision boundary \(\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{x}+c=0\}\) and the entire update sequence (so the epoch count) are identical. From a zero start \(\eta\) has no effect at all — which is why item B forbids it.

The centers are only ~1.4 units apart while the standard deviation is ~1.22 (three times the spread of Exercise 1), so the clouds overlap heavily and no straight line separates them.

Figure 4 — 2000 points; the two classes are thoroughly intermixed.

docs.title: B — Train, keeping the best weights
docs.text:
I reused the Exercise 1 perceptron unchanged (same \(\eta=0.01\), same 100-epoch cap) with pocket=True: whenever an update produces a higher full-dataset accuracy than any seen before, I copy \((\mathbf{w}, b)\) into the pocket. Because the data is not separable, the loop never stops and runs all 100 epochs.

Weights \(\mathbf{w}\) \(b\) Accuracy Final (last epoch) \([0.0361, 0.0494]\) \(-0.04\) 0.5005 Pocket (best-so-far) \([0.0068, 0.0066]\) \(-0.05\) 0.7285

The final-iterate accuracy is ~50% — no better than guessing — while the pocket holds ~72.85%, close to the best a straight line can do on this data. The best pocket accuracy was first reached at epoch 18.

docs.title: C — Figures
docs.text:
Figure 5 — The pocket boundary (green) cuts through the overlap sensibly (~72.9%); the final boundary (dashed) has drifted to the edge of the cloud, classifying almost everything as one class (~50%). Points misclassified by the pocket are circled.

Figure 6 — The current-weights accuracy (blue) oscillates around chance (0.5) and never settles; the best-so-far pocket accuracy (green) climbs and plateaus at ~0.73 by epoch ~18.

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
1. The gap between final (~50%) and pocket (~73%). On non-separable data the loop never stops updating, so the final weights are simply wherever the last mistakes left them. Figure 5 shows the final boundary sitting below the cloud (centered near \((3.5, 3.5)\)): the final \(\mathbf{w}\) is tiny (\(\Vert\mathbf{w}\Vert \approx 0.06\)) and \(b \approx -0.04\), so the line passes far from the data centroid and nearly every point lands on one side — with balanced classes that gives ~50%. The loop leaves it there because of the imbalance the hint points to: each mistake moves \(b\) by only \(\eta = 0.01\), but moves \(\mathbf{w}\) by \(\eta\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert \approx 0.01 \times 5 = 0.05\). The orientation of \(\mathbf{w}\) therefore swings ~5× faster than the offset \(b\) can travel, so \(b\) can never climb to the value \(\approx -\mathbf{w}\cdot(3.5, 3.5)\) needed to place the line through the cloud — the final line keeps getting knocked to the margin. The pocket sidesteps this entirely by remembering the best-scoring weights ever visited (73%, ≈ the best possible straight line).

2. Figure 3 vs Figure 6. In Exercise 1 the accuracy curve settles at 1.0; here it never settles — the current-weights curve bounces around 0.5 forever. The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees that if the training data is linearly separable, the algorithm finds a separating hyperplane in a finite number of updates and then stops. This dataset violates the linear-separability assumption, so there is no zero-error state to converge to: mistakes never cease, updates never stop, and the iterate keeps oscillating.

3. Do more epochs or a smaller \(\eta\) fix it? No. From the update rule, every epoch still contains misclassified (overlapping) points, so \((y-\hat{y})\ne 0\) for some samples no matter how long we train — updates continue indefinitely and the current iterate never converges; more epochs just add more oscillation, and the pocket cannot exceed the ~73% ceiling of the best straight line. A smaller \(\eta\) only rescales each step (and, per the D.3 argument, does not change which points are misclassified — predictions depend on the sign of \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b\), which \(\eta\) alone cannot flip in a way that removes the overlap); it makes the wandering finer but around the same poor region. The genuine overlap is a property of the data, not of the training budget — the only real fix is a nonlinear model (or accepting the pocket's best-line solution).

    def train(self, X, y, max_epochs=100, pocket=False):
        """Train until a full pass produces no update, or max_epochs.

        Returns a history dict (per-epoch accuracy, best-so-far accuracy, and
        update count) and the pocket record (best weights, bias, accuracy, and
        the epoch at which the best occurred).
        """
        n = len(y)
        best = {
            "w": self.w.copy(),
            "b": self.b,
            "acc": self.accuracy(X, y),
            "epoch": 0,
        }
        history = {"acc": [], "best_acc": [], "updates": []}

        for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
            updates = 0
            for i in range(n):
                xi, yi = X[i], y[i]
                y_hat = 1 if (self.w @ xi + self.b) >= 0 else 0
                error = yi - y_hat            # 0 if correct, +/-1 on a mistake
                if error != 0:
                    self.w = self.w + self.lr * error * xi
                    self.b = self.b + self.lr * error
                    updates += 1
                    if pocket:
                        acc = self.accuracy(X, y)
                        if acc > best["acc"]:
                            best = {
                                "w": self.w.copy(),
                                "b": self.b,
                                "acc": acc,
                                "epoch": epoch,
                            }

            history["acc"].append(self.accuracy(X, y))
            history["best_acc"].append(best["acc"])
            history["updates"].append(updates)

            if updates == 0:      # a clean pass: the data is separated
                break

        return history, best

docs.text: Runnable code for the Perceptron deliverable. Two well-separated 2-D Gaussian clouds are classified with a single-layer perceptron written from scratch (see perceptron.py). All randomness comes from a single fixed generator (rng = np.random.default_rng(42)); the perceptron is re-created from the same seed for each learning-rate run so the two runs differ only in $\eta$.

docs.title: A — Generate the data¶
docs.text: Class 0 $\sim \mathcal{N}([1.5,1.5], 0.5 I)$ and Class 1 $\sim \mathcal{N}([5,5], 0.5 I)$, 1000 points each. The means are ~5 units apart while the standard deviation is only ~0.7, so the clouds are cleanly separable.

docs.title: B — The perceptron¶
docs.text: The model is implemented from scratch in perceptron.py and imported above: step, predict, the $\{0,1\}$ error-driven update $w \leftarrow w + \eta (y - \hat{y}) x$, non-zero initialization (rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2), $b = 0$), $\eta = 0.01$, and stopping when a full pass produces no update (max 100 epochs).

docs.text: Runnable code for the Perceptron deliverable. The same perceptron from perceptron.py is reused unchanged on two heavily overlapping clouds. Because the data is not linearly separable the loop never stops updating, so we track the final weights (whatever the last epoch holds) and the pocket weights (the best-so-far on full-dataset accuracy).

docs.title: A — Generate the data¶
docs.text: Class 0 $\sim \mathcal{N}([3,3], 1.5 I)$ and Class 1 $\sim \mathcal{N}([4,4], 1.5 I)$. The means are now only ~1.4 units apart while the standard deviation is ~1.2, so the clouds overlap heavily and no straight line separates them.

docs.text: Reuse the Exercise 1 implementation unchanged, with $\eta = 0.01$ and the 100-epoch cap, now with pocket=True.

"""A single-layer perceptron written from scratch (no third-party model). The activation, prediction, update rule, and training loop are all implemented here with NumPy only. import numpy as np
import numpy as np In [ ]: Copied! 
def step(z):

class Perceptron:
    """Perceptron with the {0, 1} error-driven update rule.

    Prediction:  y_hat = step(w . x + b)
    Update:      w <- w + eta * (y - y_hat) * x
                 b <- b + eta * (y - y_hat)
    """

    def __init__(self, n_features, rng, lr=0.01):
        # Non-zero init: from w = 0 the learning rate only rescales w (see D.3),
        # so we draw small random weights instead.
        self.w = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=n_features)
        self.b = 0.0
        self.lr = float(lr)

    def predict(self, X):
        """Vectorised prediction for a matrix of samples (n, n_features)."""
        return step(X @ self.w + self.b)

    def accuracy(self, X, y):
        return float(np.mean(self.predict(X) == y))

    def train(self, X, y, max_epochs=100, pocket=False):
        """Train until a full pass produces no update, or max_epochs.

        Returns a history dict (per-epoch accuracy, best-so-far accuracy, and
        update count) and the pocket record (best weights, bias, accuracy, and
        the epoch at which the best occurred).
        """
        n = len(y)
        best = {
            "w": self.w.copy(),
            "b": self.b,
            "acc": self.accuracy(X, y),
            "epoch": 0,
        }
        history = {"acc": [], "best_acc": [], "updates": []}

        for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
            updates = 0
            for i in range(n):
                xi, yi = X[i], y[i]
                y_hat = 1 if (self.w @ xi + self.b) >= 0 else 0
                error = yi - y_hat            # 0 if correct, +/-1 on a mistake
                if error != 0:
                    self.w = self.w + self.lr * error * xi
                    self.b = self.b + self.lr * error
                    updates += 1
                    if pocket:
                        acc = self.accuracy(X, y)
                        if acc > best["acc"]:
                            best = {
                                "w": self.w.copy(),
                                "b": self.b,
                                "acc": acc,
                                "epoch": epoch,
                            }

            history["acc"].append(self.accuracy(X, y))
            history["best_acc"].append(best["acc"])
            history["updates"].append(updates)

            if updates == 0:      # a clean pass: the data is separated
                break

        return history, best

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
O material utiliza o mkdocs para gerar a documentação. Para visualizar a documentação, execute o comando:

mkdocs serve -o

Para subir ao GitHub Pages, execute o comando:

mkdocs gh-deploy

Esse repositório possui um workflow do GitHub Actions que executa o comando mkdocs gh-deploy sempre que houver um push na branch main. Assim, não é necessário executar esse comando manualmente. Toda vez que você fizer um push na branch main, a documentação será atualizada automaticamente no GitHub Pages.

Aviso 1

Para que o github actions funcione corretamente, é necessário que o repositório esteja configurado para que o bot github-actions[bot] tenha permissão de escrita. Você pode verificar isso nas configurações do repositório, na seção "Actions" e depois em "General". Certifique-se de que a opção "Workflow permissions" esteja definida como "Read and write permissions".

Aviso 2

Depois de publicar, caso não consiga acessar a página, verifique se o github pages está configurado corretamente. Vá até as configurações do repositório, na seção "Pages" e verifique se a branch gh-pages está selecionada como fonte. Se não estiver, selecione-a e salve as alterações.

Pay Attention

No arquivo 'mkdocs.yml, a seção site_url deve estar configurada corretamente para o seu repositório. Por exemplo, se o seu repositório estiver em https://github.com/usuario/repositorio, a seção site_url deve ser:

site_url: https://usuario.github.io/repositorio

Também, certifique-se de que a seção repo_url esteja configurada corretamente para o seu repositório. Por exemplo:

repo_url: https://github.com/usuario/repositorio
